analysis.one_liner: Requires biologic drug makers to publicly list all patents covering their drugs.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in October 2019, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in either House committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced companies that sell biologic drugs — complex drugs made from living cells, like insulin and advanced cancer therapies — to tell the Department of Health and Human Services about every patent covering their products, and to keep that list updated. HHS would then publish a free, searchable public list showing each drug's patents, how long its exclusivity periods run, and whether cheaper copies (biosimilars) can be substituted. A maker that failed to list a patent on time would lose the right to sue over it.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies trying to make cheaper biosimilar copies of biologics would benefit most: today, they can be hit with surprise patent lawsuits years after investing in a copy, and they often cannot see the full set of patents standing in their way. A public, searchable patent list would let them see those obstacles before spending money, and the threat of losing unlisted patents would make brand-name firms disclose honestly. Patients and payers benefit indirectly, because biosimilar competition is one of the few forces that pushes biologic prices down. Researchers and the public also gain access to a single government list of every approved biologic, its patents, and its exclusivity timelines — information that is currently scattered across FDA and USPTO records.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Biosimilar makers and patients facing high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers of licensed biologics would have to submit a list of every patent they believe covers their drug within 30 days of approval — and companies with products already on the market would have to file within 30 days of the bill's enactment — then keep the list current as new patents issue and old ones are invalidated.

HHS would have to publish, within one year, a single easily searchable public list showing each approved biologic's name, patents, license status, dosage form, exclusivity periods and their expiration dates, and any interchangeability determination — replacing information now scattered across agencies.

In biosimilar patent disputes, the brand manufacturer would be required to give the copycat maker the very list compiled under this bill, so the copycat would know the full patent landscape up front instead of discovering patents through litigation.

A patent that should have been listed but was not timely disclosed could no longer be used to sue for infringement, removing the brand industry's ability to spring previously hidden patents on biosimilar makers in court.

analysis.who_pays: Biologic drug manufacturers would bear the cost of compiling, filing, and updating patent lists, and would face the real financial risk of losing enforceable rights over any patent they failed to disclose on time. HHS would absorb the administrative cost of building and maintaining a continuously updated public database. Neither cost is passed directly to consumers, though manufacturers would be expected to argue the compliance burden adds expense.

drawbacks.text: Transparency alone does not lower prices. The bill requires disclosure of patents but does nothing about the underlying tactics — stacking dozens of patents on one product (a 'patent thicket') or filing follow-on patents to extend monopolies. A fully disclosed wall of 100 patents can still deter a biosimilar maker just as effectively as a hidden one.

The over-listing incentive cuts both ways: because failing to list a patent destroys the right to enforce it, manufacturers would rationally list every conceivably relevant patent. That satisfies the disclosure requirement while actually handing brand-name firms a government-published map of their patent thickets to wave at would-be competitors.

The enforcement penalty — permanently forfeiting patent rights over a listing paperwork error — is a blunt remedy that manufacturers could challenge in court, and the bill provides no funding for the new HHS database and disclosure system it mandates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but narrow: this is a transparency measure, not a price-control measure. It would meaningfully lower the legal risk and information cost facing biosimilar entrants, and public disclosure of exclusivity timelines is genuinely useful to patients, payers, and researchers. But the heaviest levers over biologic pricing — patent thickets, evergreening, FDA interchangeability barriers, and rebate practices — are untouched. The compliance cost on manufacturers is modest by industry standards. On balance a worthwhile, if incremental, pro-consumer bill; its modest scope also makes its quiet death less consequential than it would be for a price-cap bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, then parked in their subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Abigail Spanberger, a first-term Democrat, introduced the bill on October 23, 2019 with Rep. Tom Reed, a Republican, as its original cosponsor.
The same day, the Speaker's office referred it jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, meaning both would have to act before the full House could consider it.
Three days later it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; on December 18 it was also sent to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet.

That was the last recorded action. In the remaining thirteen months of the 116th Congress, neither subcommittee held a hearing, neither full committee marked up the bill, and it never received a vote of any kind before the Congress expired on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Biologic drug manufacturers kept the status quo: no duty to disclose their patent lists publicly, no risk of forfeiting patents over non-disclosure, and continued freedom to deploy undisclosed patents against biosimilar makers in litigation. Patients and biosimilar developers are no worse off than before, but they got none of the transparency the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Biologic drug manufacturers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democratic sponsor with two Republican cosponsors — but because it never reached a hearing or a vote, there is no record of how the parties would have lined up.

industries.note: Brand-name biologic makers would have to disclose every patent covering their drugs within 30 days and could permanently lose the right to enforce any patent they failed to list. That patents-and-litigation strategy is central to how these companies extend high-price exclusivity past their 12-year regulatory exclusivity period, so the bill's gain for the public comes directly at their expense.

Copycat biologic makers would get a public patent map and a legally mandated disclosure from the reference manufacturer before launching, sharply reducing the surprise-litigation risk that currently makes biosimilar entry expensive and risky. Their interest in the bill runs directly alongside patients' interest in cheaper drugs.
